''Structure generated from the source by <code>reference.py</code>; the explanations come from <code>reference_notes_plot.py</code>. Do not edit this file -- edit those and re-run.''

<code>plot</code> is a higher-level layer over [[iw]] for authoring interactive-fiction plots — one or more independent plotlines, with branching, character gating, and cross-plotline "synergy" — without hand-writing the underlying trigger machinery. You describe '''stages''' and '''transitions'''; <code>plot</code> compiles them into <code>iw</code> tracked items and trigger events.

This page is every object in <code>plot</code>, every attribute on it, and what each one is for. The structure is read out of the dataclasses themselves, so it cannot fall behind the library.

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
import iw
import plot
</syntaxhighlight>

'''None of these objects are in the world format.''' They are the description you write; <code>add_plot</code> compiles them down into the tracked items and trigger events of the <code>iw</code> layer, and it is that output the engine ever sees. So a <code>PlotStage</code> has no id and no JSON — it has an <code>internal_id</code>, which is bookkeeping for the compiler.

== Concepts ==

* '''<code>PlotStage</code>''' — a state the plot can be in. It holds no content itself; it points at the <code>PlotStageDetails</code> that apply while it is active.
* '''<code>PlotStageDetails</code>''' — one '''layer''' of stage content (<code>instruction_blocks</code>, <code>tracked_items</code>, <code>additional_effects</code>), optionally scoped to specific <code>characters</code>. Re-applied every turn the stage is active.
* '''<code>PlotTransition</code>''' — an edge from one (or more) starting stage(s) to an ending stage, fired by a player '''scenario''' and/or other conditions.
* '''<code>Plotline</code>''' — a named bundle of stages + transitions that advances independently, with its own stage tracker.
* '''<code>add_plot</code> / <code>add_plots</code>''' — compile plotline(s) into a <code>World</code>.

== How it compiles ==

Each plotline gets, namespaced by its <code>name</code>:

* a hidden '''stage tracker''' (<code>&lt;name&gt; Stage</code>) holding the id of the current stage;
* a hidden per-turn '''change gate''' (<code>&lt;name&gt; Change</code>) so the plot advances at most once per turn;
* a pool of hidden '''situation slots''' (<code>&lt;name&gt; Situation N</code>). The current stage's outgoing scenarios are written into these slots, and transitions reference them via <code>&lt;&lt;…&gt;&gt;</code> — so the engine only ever evaluates a small fixed number of situations per turn, not every scenario in the plot.

Within a plotline the trigger evaluation order is load-bearing: reset gate → start / transitions → stage triggers.

Each stage compiles to '''one trigger per content layer''': the everyone-layer first, then one per character-specific layer, each carrying an <code>ON_CHARACTER</code> condition. Because the character layers are emitted ''after'' the everyone-layer, and a <code>MODIFY_INSTRUCTION_BLOCK</code> effect is a full overwrite, a character layer naming the same block or tracked item simply wins for its characters. That cascade is the whole point: write the shared content once, the per-character delta once.

These extra triggers are cheap — they test tracked items and the chosen character, not LLM-evaluated situations, so they don't grow the situation-slot pool.

== The objects ==

=== <code>PlotStageDetails</code> ===

One layer of a plot stage's content, re-applied every turn the stage is active: the text of each instruction block, the value of each tracked item, and any extra effects. <code>characters</code> scopes the layer -- empty means everyone (see PlotStage).

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>characters</code> || `PossibleCharacter \ || list[PossibleCharacter]` || <code>[]</code> || The character(s) this layer applies to; empty means everyone.
|-
| <code>instruction_blocks</code> || <code>dict[InstructionBlock, str]</code> || <code>{}</code> || <code>{InstructionBlock: text}</code> maintained while at the stage.
|-
| <code>tracked_items</code> || <code>dict[TrackedItem, str]</code> || <code>{}</code> || <code>{TrackedItem: value}</code> maintained while at the stage.
|-
| <code>additional_effects</code> || <code>list[TriggerEffect]</code> || <code>[]</code> || Raw <code>iw</code> effects applied every turn at the stage.
|}

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
GATES = plot.PlotStage(
    # What both characters see...
    plot_details=plot.PlotStageDetails(
        instruction_blocks={block: "I stand before the keep's great sealed gates."},
    ),
    # ...and how each of them sees it. Overrides the block above, for that character only.
    character_specific_plot_details=[
        plot.PlotStageDetails(characters=warrior, instruction_blocks={block: "...They could be forced open by strength."}),
        plot.PlotStageDetails(characters=mage,    instruction_blocks={block: "...I sense a faint magic woven through the stone."}),
    ],
)
</syntaxhighlight>

A character may appear in '''at most one''' <code>character_specific_plot_details</code> entry per stage — two layers covering the same character would race to set the same blocks and items.

Characters never gate a ''stage'': every character starts at the same initial stage, and what they see there varies by layer. To gate the ''path'' a character can take, use <code>PlotTransition.characters</code>.

=== <code>PlotStage</code> ===

A state the plot can be in. Its content comes in layers: <code>plot_details</code> is what everyone sees while the plot is here (so it must not name characters), and each entry in <code>character_specific_plot_details</code> names the characters it applies to and is applied ''after'' <code>plot_details</code> -- so it can override the same instruction block or tracked item for those characters. A character may appear in at most one of these entries.

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>plot_details</code> || `PlotStageDetails \ || None` || <code>None</code> || The content everyone sees at this stage. Must '''not''' name characters.
|-
| <code>character_specific_plot_details</code> || <code>list[PlotStageDetails]</code> || <code>[]</code> || Layers applied ''on top of'' <code>plot_details</code>, each scoped to its own characters.
|-
| <code>internal_id</code> || `str \ || None` || <code>None</code> || An explicit id; otherwise the compiler assigns one.
|-
| <code>description</code> || `str \ || None` || <code>None</code> || Never emitted — it only names the stage in warnings and errors. Write one anyway.
|}

'''There is no <code>initial</code> flag.''' The plotline starts at whichever stage has no transition into it, and exactly one stage must fit that description — being the start isn't something you declare, it's what the transitions say. Every character starts there.

'''Give your stages a <code>description</code>.''' It costs nothing, and it is the difference between

<pre>
Character 'Sir Garran' can never reach stage '3' of plotline 'Plot'.
Character 'Sir Garran' can never reach stage '3' (the mage's secret passage) of plotline 'Plot'.
</pre>

The reachability and content checks below identify a stage by its <code>internal_id</code>, which is a number the compiler picked. With thirty stages in a plotline, that number tells you nothing on its own.

Both fields can be assigned after construction, so a plot file can be written in the order the story happens: '''declare a stage, wire the transition that reaches it, then write the content you arrive at.'''

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
A = plot.PlotStage()
A.plot_details = plot.PlotStageDetails(instruction_blocks={block: "the opening situation"})

B = plot.PlotStage()
A_TO_B = plot.PlotTransition(starting_stage=A, ending_stage=B, trigger_on_scenario="I do the thing")
B.plot_details = plot.PlotStageDetails(instruction_blocks={block: "the next situation"})

plot.add_plot(world, [A, B], [A_TO_B])
</syntaxhighlight>

<code>A</code> is the initial stage — not because it says so, but because nothing transitions into it.

=== <code>PlotTransition</code> ===

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>starting_stage</code> || `PlotStage \ || list[PlotStage]` || <code>required</code> || The stage, or stages, this advances from.
|-
| <code>ending_stage</code> || <code>PlotStage</code> || <code>required</code> || The stage it advances to.
|-
| <code>transition_event</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>None</code> || One-off narration (<code>TELL_AI</code>) when it fires.
|-
| <code>trigger_on_scenario</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>None</code> || The player situation that fires it, judged by the LLM.
|-
| <code>show_message</code> || `str \ || None` || <code>None</code> || One-off message shown to the player when it fires.
|-
| <code>end_game</code> || <code>bool</code> || <code>False</code> || Ends the game on this transition.
|-
| <code>can_continue</code> || `bool \ || None` || <code>None</code> || Required, and only valid, when <code>end_game</code>. <code>False</code> is a hard ending.
|-
| <code>requires</code> || <code>list[PlotStage]</code> || <code>[]</code> || Cross-plotline synergy gates — stages in ''other'' plotlines that must hold.
|-
| <code>tracked_items</code> || <code>dict[TrackedItem, str]</code> || <code>{}</code> || <code>{TrackedItem: value}</code> set '''once''', on the turn this fires.
|-
| <code>additional_conditions</code> || <code>list[TriggerCondition]</code> || <code>[]</code> || Raw <code>iw</code> conditions ANDed onto the transition.
|-
| <code>additional_effects</code> || <code>list[TriggerEffect]</code> || <code>[]</code> || Raw <code>iw</code> effects applied once, when it fires.
|-
| <code>characters</code> || `PossibleCharacter \ || list[PossibleCharacter]` || <code>[]</code> || Restricts the transition to specific characters.
|-
| <code>internal_id</code> || `str \ || None` || <code>None</code> || An explicit id; otherwise the compiler assigns one.
|}

<code>requires</code> lists <code>PlotStage</code>s belonging to '''other''' plotlines. Stages from the same plotline are '''OR''''d (any one qualifies); different plotlines are '''AND''''d (each must hold). Because plotlines are not assumed to be linear, you list every qualifying stage explicitly — there is deliberately '''no''' "this stage and everything after it" shorthand.

<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
# Unlock once Fire is adept-or-beyond AND Water is adept-or-beyond:
requires=[FIRE_ADEPT, FIRE_EXPERT, FIRE_MASTER, WATER_ADEPT, WATER_EXPERT, WATER_MASTER]
</syntaxhighlight>

=== <code>Plotline</code> ===

A named plot: stages + transitions that advance independently of other plotlines, with its own stage tracker, per-turn gate, and situation-slot pool (all namespaced by <code>name</code>). The trackers are resolved during the build (on an internal copy -- your object is left untouched); pass your own to control them, or leave them None to auto-create <code>&lt;name&gt; Stage</code> / <code>&lt;name&gt; Change</code>.

{| class="wikitable"
! attribute !! type !! default !! what it's for
|-
| <code>name</code> || <code>str</code> || <code>required</code> || Namespaces everything this plotline compiles to. Appears in warnings and errors.
|-
| <code>plot_stages</code> || <code>list[PlotStage]</code> || <code>required</code> || Every stage in the plotline.
|-
| <code>plot_transitions</code> || <code>list[PlotTransition]</code> || <code>required</code> || Every edge between them.
|-
| <code>plot_stage_tracker</code> || `TrackedItem \ || None` || <code>None</code> || The hidden tracked item holding the current stage. Filled in by the compiler.
|-
| <code>plot_change_tracker</code> || `TrackedItem \ || None` || <code>None</code> || The hidden per-turn gate. Filled in by the compiler.
|}

The two tracker fields are filled in by the compiler. You name the plotline and list its stages and transitions; the trackers are what it compiles ''to''.

== The functions ==

=== <code>add_plots(world: World, plotlines: list[Plotline], shared_gate: bool = False) -&gt; None</code> ===

Build all the given plotlines into <code>world</code>, in place: the tracked items and triggers they compile to are added to the world you pass in. The plotlines (and their stages/transitions) are deep-copied, so nothing you pass in as a plotline is modified -- but the world itself is. <code>shared_gate</code> controls the per-turn mutex (see PlotlineHandler).

Adds every plotline's tracked items and triggers to <code>world</code>, in place (it returns nothing). With <code>shared_gate=False</code> (the default) each plotline has its own per-turn gate, so plotlines advance independently and several may advance in the same turn; with <code>shared_gate=True</code> a single gate is shared, allowing at most one advance across all plotlines per turn.

=== <code>add_plot(world: World, plot_stages: list[PlotStage], plot_transitions: list[PlotTransition]) -&gt; None</code> ===

Single-plotline convenience: build one plotline named "Plot" and add it to <code>world</code>, in place. For a custom name or trackers, call add_plots with an explicit Plotline (see add_plots).

Single-plotline sugar: one plotline named <code>"Plot"</code>.

The five tutorial worlds under <code>worlds/tutorial_plot/</code> walk these features in increasing order of complexity — [../worlds/tutorial_plot/README.md <code>worlds/tutorial_plot/README.md</code>] is the guided tour.

== Stage vs. transition <code>tracked_items</code> ==

A <code>PlotStageDetails</code>' <code>instruction_blocks</code> / <code>tracked_items</code> / <code>additional_effects</code> are '''re-applied every turn''' the plot is at that stage, so their values must be idempotent ("maintained while here"). A transition's <code>tracked_items</code> are set '''once''', on the turn it fires — the same <code>{TrackedItem: value}</code> shape, but a one-shot ("this happened"). Same for <code>additional_effects</code> / <code>show_message</code> / <code>transition_event</code>.

Two things to keep in mind:

* '''Stage triggers run after transitions''', so if a transition and its <code>ending_stage</code> set the ''same'' tracked item, the stage wins on the turn the transition fires — the one-shot value never lands.
* It's a '''<code>SET</code>''', not an <code>ADD</code> — <code>{gold: "100"}</code> means "gold becomes 100", not "+100". For an increment, use <code>additional_effects</code> with a <code>TrackedItemAction.ADD</code> effect.

== Validation (raises <code>ValueError</code>) ==

* exactly one initial stage per plotline — i.e. exactly one stage with no transition into it. Two means two places to start; none means every stage is downstream of another and the plot can never begin;
* a stage's <code>plot_details</code> must not name characters;
* every <code>character_specific_plot_details</code> entry must name at least one character, and a character may appear in at most one of them per stage;
* <code>can_continue</code> set if and only if <code>end_game</code>;
* every referenced character must exist in <code>world.possibleCharacters</code>;
* <code>requires</code> must reference stages that exist in some plotline;
* each stage / transition belongs to exactly one plotline;
* a transition has at least one starting stage, and only references stages of its own plotline;
* '''no dead content''' — see Reachability.

== Reachability ==

<code>add_plot(s)</code> searches, for each playable character, every way that character could ever advance the plot, and refuses to build a world containing content they can never see.

'''Errors''' (dead content — always a bug):

{| class="wikitable"
|-
| a stage '''no character''' can reach || you forgot to wire it up, or its only routes in are impossible
|-
| a '''transition that can never fire''' for anyone || its starting stage is out of reach, or its <code>requires</code> can never hold
|-
| a '''character-specific layer''' for a character who can never reach its stage || content written for the wrong character
|-
| a '''character-gated transition''' that can never fire for a character it names || that character can't reach its starting stage, or can't satisfy its <code>requires</code> from there
|}

'''Warnings''' (<code>PlotReachabilityWarning</code> — often deliberate): a stage some ''particular'' character can never reach. A character-gated branch is unreachable to everyone else by design, so this is a nudge, not a bug. It only escalates to an error if you also wrote character-specific content there.

== Content warnings ==

Nothing ever ''clears'' an instruction block or a tracked item — it holds whatever was last written to it, and stage content is re-written every turn the stage is active. Two consequences are easy to trip over, so <code>add_plot(s)</code> warns (<code>PlotContentWarning</code>) about both. Neither raises: both can be deliberate.

'''Two plotlines writing the same block or item.''' They don't take turns — ''both'' write it every turn, so whichever plotline's stage trigger is emitted last wins and the other's value never survives a turn. Usually one of them meant to have its own block. In <code>worlds/tutorial_plot/5_multiple_plotlines/</code> each art owns a block named after it, which is why that world is quiet.

'''A stage that leaves alone what an earlier stage sets.''' If stage 1 sets <code>Gold</code> and stage 3 — reachable from it — doesn't, then arriving at stage 3 leaves <code>Gold</code> still showing stage 1's value, describing a situation the plot has already left. The usual fix is for every stage in a plotline to write the same set of blocks and items.

This is directional: it only fires for stages '''downstream''' of the one that writes the target. A tracked item introduced at the final stage has nothing after it, so it's silent. The downstream walk deliberately ignores character gates and <code>requires</code> — a stale value is a hazard on any path the plot could take, not just one a particular character can force.

== How the search works ==

The engine's <code>requires</code> gates couple plotlines together: whether a Steam transition can fire depends on where Fire and Water currently stand. So reachability is '''not''' a question about one plotline's graph — a state is the tuple of ''one current stage per plotline'', and the search is a walk over reachable tuples. Nothing ever forces a plotline to advance (it sits at its stage until one of its own transitions fires), which is what lets a character hold one plotline still while advancing another to line up a synergy gate — and what makes the walk a plain BFS.

Searching the full product of every plotline would be exponential (80,000 states in <code>worlds/tutorial_plot/5_multiple_plotlines/</code>). It doesn't have to: each plotline is decided against its '''cluster''' — itself plus everything it transitively <code>requires</code>. That cluster is closed (no transition inside it reads a plotline outside it), so the rest of the world provably cannot affect it:

{| class="wikitable"
! deciding !! cluster searched !! states
|-
| <code>Fire</code> || <code>{Fire}</code> || 5
|-
| <code>Steam</code> || <code>{Fire, Water, Steam}</code> || 50
|-
| <code>Victory</code> || <code>{Fire, Water, Earth, Air, Victory}</code> || 1,250
|}

Fire's five stages are verified without ever considering how far along Air is. The largest cluster in that world is 1,250 states — 64× smaller than the monolithic product — and the whole check runs in milliseconds.

<code>trigger_on_scenario</code> and <code>additional_conditions</code> are assumed '''always satisfiable''' — they're LLM- and tracked-item-judged, so we can't decide them. Everything we ''can'' decide is decided exactly: character gates, the stage graph, and <code>requires</code>. A transition with <code>end_game=True, can_continue=False</code> is treated as terminal — it fires, but nothing advances after it, so anything only reachable "past" a hard ending is correctly reported as dead.

If a plotline's cluster exceeds <code>_MAX_SEARCH_STATES</code> (200,000), the search gives up on that cluster and warns that its reachability could not be determined, rather than reporting findings it can't stand behind. Nothing in it is checked.

== Notes ==

* '''Inputs are not mutated.''' <code>add_plot(s)</code> deep-copies the world and the plotlines, so your <code>PlotStage</code> / <code>PlotTransition</code> / <code>Plotline</code> objects are unchanged and safe to reuse across builds.
* The trigger-ordering and "fires every turn" behaviours rely on the game engine's evaluation semantics; the shapes here are verified structurally against exported worlds, so validate a built world in the engine before relying on it.
